Uber, Zipline partner on US drone delivery for Uber Eats

Aug 17 (Reuters) - Uber Technologies and Zipline announced a partnership on Monday to bring autonomous drone delivery to Uber Eats customers across the United States. The tie-up was accompanied by Uber making a strategic investment in the drone delivery company. • The companies said they aim to reach 1 million drone deliveries per day by the end of 2029, with the first deliveries beginning later this year.

• The service will first launch in Zipline's existing U.S. markets before expanding to dozens of additional cities. • Uber declined to comment on Reuters' request seeking financial details of its investment in Zipline. • Zipline, which operates in four continents, has made 2 million deliveries so far. The company was most recently valued at $7.6 billion after raising $800 million earlier this year. • The Zipline deal is similar to Uber's partnership with drone firm Flytrex last year, which also included an investment. • Zipline has been expanding its U.S. footprint, with commercial partners including Walmart, as well as more than a dozen restaurant brands such as Panera, Chipotle and Wendy's. (Reporting by Akash Sriram in Bengaluru; Editing by Shilpi Majumdar)

item.title: Jane Street $15 billion loss July Situational Awareness hedge fund
item.description: The trading firm's first negative month since 2016 came as Leopold Aschenbrenner's fund shed most of its assets in a distressed sale
item.dc:creator: Cris Tolomia
item.content:encoded:
Jane Street $15 billion loss July Situational Awareness hedge fund

Jane Street $15 billion loss July Situational Awareness hedge fund · Quartz · Bloomberg / Getty Images Cris Tolomia Mon, August 17, 2026 at 9:11 AM EDT 2 min read

Jane Street took a $15 billion hit in July tied to its stake in AI-focused hedge fund Situational Awareness and long positions in technology stocks that declined during a broad market selloff, according to Reuters . July represented a milestone in the wrong direction for Jane Street — its trading revenue had not gone negative in any single month since 2016.

In a note to employees, Jane Street executives called July a "bad month" and attributed part of the damage to a steep drawdown at Situational Awareness. "We have an investment in Situational Awareness, an externally managed AI-focused hedge fund, that became large by performing well in the first half of the year," the note said. "They had a large drawdown that left our stake about flat on the year, but still up over the entire period we have been invested." The firm said hedges it had put in place provided little protection because losses in AI stocks accumulated throughout the month rather than in a sudden drop. Jane Street's pain extended beyond AI names, with long bets on Asian stocks outside the AI sector — many of which had been strong performers in prior months — also turning against the firm. Despite the July setback, Jane Street's cumulative trading revenue for the year had climbed past $40 billion, surpassing the $39.6 billion it booked across the entirety of 2025. Since the losses, Jane Street said it has wound down a substantial share of exposure in the positions that drove the damage and has also grown more cautious across other parts of its book.

Situational Awareness, which is run by Leopold Aschenbrenner, a former OpenAI researcher, lost roughly $35 billion in assets after margin calls from prime brokers forced a distressed sale of its publicly traded holdings to Ken Griffin's Citadel. The fund, which peaked at $45 billion at the start of July, saw its assets drop to roughly $10 billion after Citadel acquired its leveraged positions — including SK Hynix and CoreWeave — at below-market prices. Situational Awareness had used as much as 400% leverage and built its public portfolio around bets on AI infrastructure companies. In the weeks that followed, Aschenbrenner moved to rebuild by making a $400 million investment in an undisclosed private company , the first public signal of his intentions after the near-collapse. In a letter to investors, he pledged to draw lessons from the experience. Jane Street did not respond to a request for comment, according to Reuters.
